topic_editions.edition_state: Built locally from published upstream records
topic_editions.orientation: This state-of-evidence review treats Advanced Manufacturing as a four-horizon research program rather than a collection of headlines. The central research problem is to distinguish installed equipment, qualified lines, receiver-accepted output and dependable production. Announced capacity and isolated delivery milestones are useful chronology, but neither supplies a stable account of yield, rework, downtime, workforce qualification or customer acceptance. The workbench currently contains 3 missions with exact Phase 120 packet joins and 1 with an acquisition-coverage gap. That split describes preparation, not truth or importance: all four missions remain unadjudicated. The review reads the evidence in the inherited Phase 124 order, connects it to 4 exact Phase 125 annotations and 4 source identities, and preserves each Phase 126 requirement test. Its purpose is to show what the corpus can orient, where definitions or denominators break, and which exact record would most improve the next review. Readers can use this review to see why production announcements and industrial-policy totals should not be mistaken for dependable capacity. It also identifies where official program records support a bounded statement and where only a company or program-level account is available.
canonical_synthesis: The Published shelf shows advanced manufacturing as a coupled production system rather than a collection of factory announcements. Drive48 reports an operating training facility and more than 2,000 graduates; Monaghan Medical's certified project record pairs completed investment with a current employment count; the F-15EX record fixes delivery to a named receiving wing; and the KC-46 plan separates three availability workstreams. Together they show that facilities, workforce, delivered assets and operational readiness are related but non-interchangeable forms of evidence.

The central editorial conclusion is therefore procedural: capacity should be traced through facility readiness, workforce preparation, process qualification, accepted output and performance in the receiving system. A completed building or funded expansion can remove a constraint without proving stable yield, dependable throughput or mission availability.
topic_editions.strongest_current_evidence: The corpus is unusually rich in named production programs, audited oversight, delivery records, local workforce evidence and explicit cross-series holds. Those records make it possible to compare the shape of evidence chains while preserving the fact that MEP client surveys, aircraft deliveries, semiconductor construction and medical-device manufacturing use different entities and denominators. topic_editions.orientation: This state-of-evidence review treats Quantum as a four-horizon research program rather than a collection of headlines. Quantum research must keep computing, sensing, communications and cryptographic migration distinct. Post-quantum standards respond to a future threat; they are not evidence that a quantum computer or sensor achieved an operating outcome. The workbench currently contains 3 missions with exact Phase 120 packet joins and 1 with an acquisition-coverage gap. That split describes preparation, not truth or importance: all four missions remain unadjudicated. The review reads the evidence in the inherited Phase 124 order, connects it to 4 exact Phase 125 annotations and 5 source identities, and preserves each Phase 126 requirement test. Its purpose is to show what the corpus can orient, where definitions or denominators break, and which exact record would most improve the next review. Readers can use this review to see that the evidence gap is explicit rather than hidden. It preserves useful post-quantum material in its proper domain while directing quantum-outcome research toward official benchmark and accepted-use records.
canonical_synthesis: The quantum shelf is deliberately centered on post-quantum cryptography. It separates final 2024 standards, NIST's 2025 selection of HQC as a backup algorithm, preliminary PIV credential specifications and federal migration plans with dated transitions. This gives the topic an implementation spine rather than relying on generalized quantum-computing expectations.

The resulting question is not whether an algorithm has been selected, but whether organizations know which systems and dependencies are exposed, acquire interoperable implementations, validate them, complete cutover and retire vulnerable legacy components. A backup-algorithm selection is not yet a standard, and a working draft is not a deployed credential system.
